newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani politicians wind up election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani politicians wind up election campaign.

text.p: Pakistani politicians hurled themselves into a final day of election campaigning on Saturday, but voters seemed unconvinced that they will tackle rampant corruption or solve Pakistan's economic problems.
Pakistanis go to the polls on Monday to choose between two former prime ministers, Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, who have both seen their governments sacked on corruption charges.
Or they can opt for former cricket star Imran Khan, who has campaigned against corruption, but whose untried party pollsters say will win few, if any, seats in the National Assembly.
Some will give their votes to religious, regional or ethnic parties such as the Karachi-based Mohajir National Movement (MQM), target of a fierce crackdown under Bhutto's government.
Opinion polls put Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) clearly ahead of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP), whose government was fired by President Farooq Leghari on November 5.
Leghari alleged that his former ally's three-year rule had been tainted by corruption, nepotism, extra-judicial killings, contempt for the judiciary and many other abuses.
Bhutto, who was addressing six rallies in a last hectic whirl of campaigning in Lahore on Saturday, denies all the charges, saying Leghari is at the heart of a dark conspiracy.
Her imprisoned husband has accused the president of making corruption allegations against him to get at his wife.
In BBC interview to be broadcast on Saturday, Asif Ali Zardari said: "They just have to attack somebody. They had to make a target and they have to build around it."

Zardari, who is awaiting trial on charges of conspiracy to murder Bhutto's brother, told the BBC in the interview that Leghari and government advisers had found it difficult to make people believe that there was "something wrong" with his wife.
"So who do they have to make believe that there is something wrong with her? It's the husband, because if you hit the husband, you're hitting home," he said.
Zardari said he was known for years in Pakistan business circles as "Mr Ten Percent", but that nothing had been proved.
However, the Supreme Court on Wednesday upheld Leghari's action as justified and threw out Bhutto's appeal against her dismissal, clearing the way for the polls to go ahead.
Sharif, confident of victory, told about 10,000 roaring supporters at a rally in Rawalpindi, 20 km (12 miles) south of Islamabad on Friday, that Bhutto's time had ended.

But the campaign has sparked little enthusiasm among a public deeply disenchanted with a political class perceived as consistently failing to deliver clean, honest government since the return of parliamentary democracy in 1988.
"I'm going to vote for Imran," said a woman voter in Islamabad. "I dislike him, but if you look at the sort of people who sit in the National Assembly, he has more potential."
Political analysts predict a turn-out possibly as low as 20 percent, compared to 69 percent in 1988 and 40 percent in 1993.

They attribute this partly to preoccupation with the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, now at its climax, but also to public disgust at the politicians and bureaucrats credited with getting Pakistan labelled as one of the world's most corrupt countries.
"Clearly corruption was beginning to eat the very fabric of our society and bring about an economic collapse," caretaker Commerce Minister Zubair Khan told Reuters this week.
"It was determining the formulation of policy, the selection of projects and then it was affecting implementation," he said.
